A population grows when births outnumber deaths and shrinks when they do not. That
is the entire mechanism, and everything else on this page follows from it.

The equation for it is

> **dN/dt = r N (1 − N/K)**

and the two letters in it, **r** and **K**, are the ones you will be asked about in
every exam question and every management report. Neither of them is something an
organism has. They are both **consequences** of birth and death rates — which is why
this page gives you no slider for either one.

## 1. Births, deaths, and where they balance

Set four numbers: how fast individuals reproduce and die when there is plenty of
room, how much crowding matters, and how many arrive to begin with. Then watch what
the population does — and watch **r** and **K** appear in the readouts underneath
without you ever having touched them.

::: {.pd-tool}
::: {.pd-controls #pd-logistic-controls}
:::
::: {.pd-chart #pd-logistic-chart}
:::
::: {.pd-readout #pd-logistic-readout}
:::

### Reading the two charts

**The trajectory** is the familiar S-curve. The dashed grey line at your target is
the number to aim at; the band around it turns green when **K** lands inside it.

**The two bars underneath are the part the S-curve cannot show you.** They are the
*total* births and deaths per year at whichever moment the slider is parked on, and
the gap between their ends is `dN/dt` — the left-hand side of the equation, drawn.
Drag the slider from year zero to the end and watch what happens: the birth bar
starts far ahead, the two converge, and at **K** they are **equal and both still
long**. A population at carrying capacity is not resting. It is replacing itself as
fast as it can, and the readout tells you how many individuals per year that costs.

**Births and deaths** (the first tab) shows the same story as two per-capita rates.
`b(N)` slopes down or stays flat, `d(N)` climbs, and **where the two lines cross is
K**. Nothing is capping the population from outside; it stops growing because at that
density a typical individual has exactly as many offspring as it has chances of
dying.

**How the fit works** (the second tab) is the statistics. Divide the equation by N
and you get the per-capita growth rate:

> **(1/N) dN/dt = r − (r/K) N**

which is a **straight line** in N. So an ecologist with nothing but a column of
counts can plot the growth rate against the population size, draw the best line
through it, and read the answers straight off: the line's **height at zero is r**,
and the point where it **crosses zero is K**. That is what the gold line is doing,
and it is the same fit as the dashed curve on the trajectory chart — the same
estimate, drawn in the coordinates where it happens to be a line.

::: {.pd-try}
In class: hit 500

1. **Tune the rates until K reads 500.** Any way you like. The band goes green when
   you are there.
2. **Write down your b₀ and d₀** — you will be asked for them.
3. Note what you did *not* do: you never set K, and you never set the lifespan.

Then look around the room. Everybody hit 500 and almost nobody did it with your
numbers, which is the point of Section 2.
:::

::: {.pd-try}
Things to try

- **Hit 500 twice, once with tiny rates and once with big ones.** Try `b₀ = 0.12,
  d₀ = 0.02, δ = 0.20`, then `b₀ = 1.40, d₀ = 0.60, δ = 1.60`. Both land on K = 500,
  and you need all three numbers each time — hitting a target with three knobs
  leaves you a whole family of ways to do it. Now check the mean lifespan: 8.3 years
  in the first, about eight months in the second. Same carrying capacity, one a
  population of trees and the other of voles.
- **Park the slider at the far right and watch the two bars.** They are equal, and
  neither is anywhere near zero. Then read "turnover at K": that many individuals
  are born and die every year, forever, with the total never moving.
- **Turn the crowding slider down to zero.** K is gone, and the readout says why:
  with nothing multiplying the bracket, `dN/dt = rN` is the exponential, and no
  population obeys it for long.
- **Set d₀ above b₀.** Deaths win even in an empty landscape, and there is no
  positive equilibrium to find at any density.
- **Start above your carrying capacity** — leave the rates alone and drag N₀ past
  500. The population *falls* to the same place it used to climb to. K is not a
  ceiling that stops growth; it is the level both directions run towards. Watch the
  two bars while you do it: above K the death bar is the longer one.
- **Raise observation noise to 10 %**, then press "New census" a few times. The
  population never changed — only the counting did. Watch how far r̂ and K̂ move
  anyway, and check whether the ✓ in the scorecard survives it.
- **Set the census interval to 5 years and the target to 1000.** Fewer counts, worse
  estimate. When you plan a monitoring programme, *how often you count* is a decision
  with consequences.
- **Open "Also let crowding reduce births"** and trade δ for β, keeping K at 500.
  The trajectory does not move at all. The curve cannot tell you *which* vital rate
  crowding acts on — for that you have to go out and measure births and deaths
  separately, not just count individuals.
:::

## 2. Everyone's answer at once

Five students who all hit 500, on one chart with a fixed axis.

::: {.pd-tool}
::: {.pd-controls #pd-overlay-controls}
:::
::: {.pd-chart #pd-overlay-chart}
:::
:::

Every line ends in the same place, because that is what everyone aimed at. No two
get there at the same speed, because **nobody was aiming at r** — it came along for
the ride as `b₀ − d₀`. Read down the table: the K column is constant and every other
column is not.

This is worth being uncomfortable about for a moment. If many different populations
share a carrying capacity, then **K is not a fact about a species** — you cannot look
it up. It is a property of a particular population's birth and death rates in a
particular environment, and it moves whenever anything moves those rates: a drought,
a new predator, a fertiliser, a warmer decade. Half of applied ecology is arguing
about what K is for something, and this is why those arguments are hard.

## Notes and further reading

### What this simulation leaves out

::: {.pd-howto}

**Nothing here is random except the counting.** The population follows the smooth
curve exactly, and the noise slider only blurs the observer's view of it. Real
populations are pushed around by chance in two further ways this page does not
simulate: **demographic** stochasticity, because births and deaths are whole-number
events that can go the wrong way in a small population, and **environmental**
stochasticity, because good years and bad years move the rates themselves. The
first is why small populations go extinct even when their growth rate is positive
— which no curve on this page can show you.

**Every individual is identical and immortal until it isn't.** There are no ages, no
sexes, no juveniles too young to breed and no elders past breeding. `b₀` and `d₀`
apply to everyone equally. Real populations have age structure, and it makes them
lag: a population that has just been harvested keeps declining for years afterwards
because the breeding adults are gone. Nothing here has that memory.

**The response to crowding is instantaneous and it is a straight line.** Both are
choices. Add a delay and the population overshoots K and oscillates around it, which
is what deer irruptions and lemming cycles look like; make crowding non-linear and
the shape of the S-curve changes. The logistic is the simplest thing that stops
growing, not the most realistic one.

**There is no space.** No territories, no dispersal, no refuges — crowding is a
single number that every individual feels equally, no matter where it is. That is
also why the individuals here are never drawn as dots on a map: it would suggest a
geography the model does not have.

**The fit is honest about one thing and quietly biased about another.** When the
counts carry no information about a carrying capacity, it says *not identifiable*
rather than inventing a number. But sampling error also flattens the fitted line,
which pushes r̂ down and K̂ up by a few per cent — visible if you raise the noise and
watch the scorecard. Both behaviours are real properties of real fits to real census
data.

:::

### Where to read more

**Written to be read:**

- **Gotelli, N.J. (2008).** *A Primer of Ecology*, 4th ed., chs. 1–2. The clearest
  short treatment of exactly this model, including the vital-rate derivation used
  here.
- **Hone, J. (2007).** *Wildlife Damage Control.* For what happens when somebody has
  to act on an estimated K.

**The papers behind the pieces:**

- Verhulst, P.-F. (1838). Notice sur la loi que la population suit dans son
  accroissement. *Correspondance Mathématique et Physique* 10:113–121.
- Pearl, R. & Reed, L.J. (1920). On the rate of growth of the population of the
  United States since 1790. *PNAS* 6:275–288.
- Gause, G.F. (1934). *The Struggle for Existence.* Williams & Wilkins. The
  *Paramecium* cultures that first fitted this equation to a real population.
- Efron, B. (1979). Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife.
  *Annals of Statistics* 7:1–26. Where the confidence intervals on this page
  come from.
